blocks.content: In the previous chapter, we looked at Association where objects simply know about each other and interact freely. Each object lived its own independent life.
But sometimes the relationship goes a little deeper. Sometimes one object acts as a container and another acts as its content. One is the whole, the other is a part of it.
Think of a library and its books, a company and its employees, or a shopping cart and its items.

This is exactly what Aggregation models. It takes the concept of association one step further by defining a clear "whole-part" relationship between two objects while still allowing each part to exist on its own.
1. What is Aggregation?
Aggregation is a "has-a" relationship where one class contains other objects but those objects don't depend on the container to exist.
The container brings the parts together, but each part has its own independent life outside of it.
Key Characteristics:

["No ownership the container holds references to its parts but doesn't own them. Parts exist on their own.
","Parts survive alone remove the container and the parts are still alive. Delete a playlist and the songs still exist.
","No lifecycle control the container didn't create the parts and can't destroy them either.
","Parts can be shared the same object can belong to multiple containers at the same time.
","Independent existence both sides are created and destroyed completely separately from each other.
"]
items: No ownership the container holds references to its parts but doesn't own them. Parts exist on their own.
Parts survive alone remove the container and the parts are still alive. Delete a playlist and the songs still exist.
No lifecycle control the container didn't create the parts and can't destroy them either.
Parts can be shared the same object can belong to multiple containers at the same time.
Independent existence both sides are created and destroyed completely separately from each other.

blocks.content: Objects grouped together for a purpose but free to exist on their own. That is aggregation.
Real-World Analogy
Think of a sports team and its players:

["A team has many players.","Players are not owned by the team they are simply part of it.","If the team is disbanded, the players still exist and can join other teams.","A player can even be part of multiple teams at the same time a national team and a club team for example."]
items: A team has many players.
Players are not owned by the team they are simply part of it.
If the team is disbanded, the players still exist and can join other teams.
A player can even be part of multiple teams at the same time a national team and a club team for example.

blocks.content: This is aggregation in action. The team and its players are connected, but neither controls the other's existence. The team can come and go, and so can the players completely independently of each other.
2. UML Representation
In UML class diagrams, aggregation is represented by a hollow diamond (◊) on the "whole" side of the relationship. The diamond connects to the class that contains or references the other objects.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245769645-939f2dea.png

["Library holds references to multiple Book objects. The 1 to * multiplicity means one library can group many books.","Book is an independent entity with its own data (title, author, isbn). It doesn't know which library is referencing it.","The hollow diamond (o--) on the Library side is the UML notation for aggregation. It signals that Library is the \"whole\" and Book is the \"part\" but the books are not owned by the library."]
items: Library holds references to multiple Book objects. The 1 to * multiplicity means one library can group many books.
Book is an independent entity with its own data (title, author, isbn). It doesn't know which library is referencing it.
The hollow diamond (o--) on the Library side is the UML notation for aggregation. It signals that Library is the "whole" and Book is the "part" but the books are not owned by the library.

blocks.content: 3. Code Example

Let's model a real-world aggregation: the relationship between a Library and its Book objects. A library has books, but the books are independent entities. If the library shuts down, the books still exist and can be moved anywhere else.
Step 1: Build the Book Class
Books are created completely independently. They don't know anything about which library holds them.
Step 2: Build the Library Class
The library receives books from outside it never creates them itself. It simply holds references to them.
Step 3: Run in Main
Books are created first on their own, then passed into the library. Notice the library never calls new Book() anywhere inside it.
Step 5: Understanding the Output
cityLibrary.showBooks() is called which prints the library name firstCity Library. Then it loops through the book list and prints each title and author one by one.

The most important thing to notice here is that the library never created these books they were built outside and simply handed in. If you delete cityLibrary right now, b1 and b2 are still sitting in memory completely unaffected and ready to be passed into any other library. That is aggregation in action.
4. Why Aggregation Matters in OOP
Reusability The same Book can exist in multiple libraries at the same time. Write it once, use it anywhere.
Flexibility Change how Library works without touching Book at all. Loose connection means less risk.
Mirrors Real Life Libraries have books. Teams have players. Aggregation makes your code feel natural and intuitive.
Bad → Good → Great

["Bad Library creates and destroys its own books internally. Tight coupling. Hard to change. Hard to test.
","Good Library receives books that were created outside and simply holds references to them. Clean and independent.
","Great The book list is injected through the constructor. Swap any books in and out freely. Easy to test, easy to maintain. This is the best approach.
"]
items: Bad Library creates and destroys its own books internally. Tight coupling. Hard to change. Hard to test.
Good Library receives books that were created outside and simply holds references to them. Clean and independent.
Great The book list is injected through the constructor. Swap any books in and out freely. Easy to test, easy to maintain. This is the best approach.

blocks.content: 5. Example: School Management System

Let's build a system that demonstrates aggregation across multiple classes. A school manages teachers, subjects, classrooms, and students. The relationships show how parts can be shared across multiple wholes and how deleting a whole leaves its parts completely intact.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245769879-c82af0f0.png
Here's how the classes connect:

["Teacher is an independent entity that teaches subjects.","Subject belongs to a Teacher but exists independently of any classroom.","Classroom aggregates multiple Subject objects. The same subject can appear in different classrooms.","Student aggregates multiple Classroom objects. Removing a student doesn't destroy the classrooms.","School holds the master collection of all subjects, independent of any classroom or student."]
items: Teacher is an independent entity that teaches subjects.
Subject belongs to a Teacher but exists independently of any classroom.
Classroom aggregates multiple Subject objects. The same subject can appear in different classrooms.
Student aggregates multiple Classroom objects. Removing a student doesn't destroy the classrooms.
School holds the master collection of all subjects, independent of any classroom or student.

blocks.content: Step 1: Build the Teacher Class
Simple and independent. A teacher exists on their own.
Step 2: Build the Subject Class
A subject knows its teacher but doesn't know anything about which classroom it belongs to.
Step 3: Build the Classroom Class
A classroom groups subjects together but never creates or destroys them.
Step 4: Build the Student Class
A student can enroll in multiple classrooms. Removing a student doesn't affect the classrooms at all.
Step 5: Build the School Class
The master collection. Holds all subjects independently of any classroom or student.

6. Why This Design Works

Subjects are shared across classrooms. English appears in both Class A and Class B both reference the exact same Subjectobject. Update the subject once and both classrooms see the change automatically.

Removing a classroom doesn't destroy subjects. When Class A is removed, the school still has all 4 subjects and Class B is completely unaffected. The classroom was just a container of references not an owner.
The school is the authoritative source. Subjects exist in School independently of any classroom. Classrooms are simply views over the school's data.

Students own classrooms but classrooms don't own subjects. Aggregation works at two levels here Student aggregates Classroom and Classroom aggregates Subject. At every level the parts survive the deletion of the whole.
